title: Relational Databases, Primary Keys, Foreign Keys, and Constraints
learningObjectives: Explain relations, rows, columns, and the role of a relational schema.
Choose primary and candidate keys based on identity and business rules.
Distinguish primary, foreign, unique, check, and not-null constraints.
Explain how constraints protect invariants under concurrent writes.
Diagnose when a constraint should be immediate, deferred, or represented differently.

mentalModel.text: Imagine an orders screen that shows a customer's name beside every order. If we save the name and email on every order, a later email change means fixing many rows. A relational database helps us store each kind of fact in the right table and connect those tables with keys. Constraints stop invalid data, even when two requests arrive at once.

blocks.text: Start with the facts the application needs to remember, not the fields that happen to appear on one screen.

Think of a table as a list of facts about one kind of thing. A customers table describes customers; an orders table describes orders. One customer can have many orders, so each order points to its customer instead of copying every customer detail.
From a screen to a model

blocks.problem: An order screen shows order number, customer name, customer email, and total.
reasoning: The order number and date describe the order; name and email describe the customer.
Store customer details once in customers and refer to that customer from orders using customer_id.
Join the tables when the screen needs both sets of facts. Keep a purchase-time snapshot only when history requires it.
blocks.outcome: Separate tables by the facts they own. A JOIN can assemble a screen without making every order a second source of truth for customer details.

blocks.title: A table is not automatically normalized
blocks.content: Putting every field visible on one screen into one table may duplicate facts and create update anomalies. Start from entities, relationships, and invariants—not from page layout.

concepts.title: Primary keys, candidate keys, and business identity

blocks.text: A primary key answers 'which row is this?' A UNIQUE constraint answers 'which values must not be repeated?'.

A primary key is a row's stable ID. A candidate key is any smallest set of columns that could uniquely identify the row. For example, user_id might be the primary key while email has a UNIQUE rule. Email can change, so it is not always a good permanent ID.

rows: Surrogate key (e.g. BIGINT or UUID)
Stable identity; decouples references from business meaning; convenient for relationships.
Does not enforce business uniqueness by itself; still add UNIQUE constraints for natural business keys.
Natural key (e.g. ISO country code)
Meaningful and may already be unique by domain rules.
Can change, be wide, be inconsistently formatted, or encode assumptions that later prove false.
Composite key (e.g. order_id + line_number)
Can express identity that exists only within a parent or scope.
Every referencing relation may need multiple columns; key changes can be expensive.

blocks.text: Email is not always a safe primary key

blocks.problem: A user has user_id = 42 and email = 'sam@example.com'. The user changes email next month.
reasoning: Other tables can keep referring to user_id = 42.
A UNIQUE constraint on email can still prevent two users from claiming the same email.
If email were the primary key, changing it would also require updating every foreign key that refers to it.
blocks.outcome: Use a stable primary key for row identity and separate UNIQUE constraints for business rules such as email uniqueness.

blocks.text: A foreign key lets the database enforce that a reference points to a real parent row.

A foreign key is a database-enforced link to another row. If orders.customer_id points to customers.id, the database can reject an order for a customer who does not exist. PostgreSQL does not automatically index the child column, so add one when queries or parent deletes need it.

blocks.title: A parent-child relationship

blocks.text: The SQL above uses `ON DELETE RESTRICT`. That choice matters when someone tries to delete a customer who still has orders. Before choosing an action, ask: if the parent row goes away, what should happen to each dependent row? The database can enforce that decision for you.
### 1. RESTRICT / NO ACTION: do not allow the delete

Imagine customer 12 has three orders. You try to delete customer 12. With `RESTRICT`, PostgreSQL refuses because those orders still point to that customer. The customer and orders remain unchanged. This is useful when the child records must not be left pointing at a missing parent.

blocks.title: Deletion is blocked while orders exist
blocks.source:
DELETE FROM customers WHERE id = 12;
-- Fails while orders still reference customer 12

blocks.text: `RESTRICT` and `NO ACTION` often look the same: both prevent an invalid reference. The difference is timing. `RESTRICT` blocks the operation immediately. A deferrable `NO ACTION` constraint can postpone the check until the end of the transaction, which can help when a sequence of changes temporarily breaks the relationship but restores it before commit.
### 2. CASCADE: delete the dependent rows too

Imagine a shopping cart and its cart items. A cart item has no useful life once its cart is deleted. With `ON DELETE CASCADE`, deleting the cart also deletes its cart items. You do not need a separate DELETE for every item.

blocks.title: A child that belongs only to its parent

blocks.text: That convenience can be dangerous for orders, payments, invoices, or audit records. Those records may need to survive even if a customer account is closed. Do not use CASCADE just because it avoids writing another query; use it only when the child truly has no independent lifecycle and deletion is the intended business rule.
### 3. SET NULL: keep the child, clear the relationship

Imagine a support ticket assigned to an employee. If that employee leaves, you may want to keep the ticket but make it unassigned. `ON DELETE SET NULL` keeps the ticket and changes `assigned_employee_id` to NULL. The column must allow NULL, and the application must know what an unassigned ticket means.

blocks.title: Keep the ticket after its assignee is deleted

blocks.text: This is not appropriate for the `orders.customer_id` column shown earlier because it is `NOT NULL`. It would also be a poor choice if you must preserve who handled a ticket for audit reasons; in that case, retain the employee record or store an appropriate historical snapshot.
### 4. SET DEFAULT: replace the reference with a fallback

Imagine support tickets are assigned to a team. When a team is removed, you want its tickets to move to a special team called `Unassigned`. `ON DELETE SET DEFAULT` replaces the deleted team's ID with the column's default value. That default must still point to a real team, or the foreign-key check will fail.

blocks.title: Use a valid fallback team

blocks.text: `SET DEFAULT` does not mean 'accept any missing parent'. It substitutes the default, then the foreign key still checks that the new value exists. This is useful only when the fallback has a clear meaning and is guaranteed to exist.
### Compare the choices

columns: What happens to the child row?
rows: RESTRICT
Parent deletion is rejected while child rows refer to it.
An order must keep its customer reference valid.
NO ACTION
The reference must be valid when the constraint is checked; a deferrable constraint can check at transaction end.
A multi-step transaction temporarily changes relationships before restoring validity.
CASCADE
The child row is deleted along with the parent.
Cart items that have no independent life outside their cart.
SET NULL
The child stays, but its foreign-key value becomes NULL.
A ticket stays after its optional assignee is removed.
SET DEFAULT
The child stays, and its foreign-key value changes to the column default; that default must reference a real parent.
A ticket moves to a permanent 'Unassigned' team.

blocks.title: Choose based on what the data means
blocks.content: Before selecting an action, ask what the child record represents and whether it must survive the parent's deletion. For customer orders, preserving history is usually more important than automatically deleting the order. For temporary cart items, cascading deletion may be exactly right. The database action should match the product's retention and lifecycle rules.

blocks.title: CASCADE is a business decision
blocks.content: It is not merely a convenience. A cascade can remove a large graph of data. Use it when the child has no independent lifecycle and deletion is intended to propagate.

blocks.problem: An API inserts an order with customer_id = 900, but no customer with id 900 exists.
reasoning: The application may have checked earlier, but the customer could have been deleted before the insert.
An enforced foreign key checks the relationship at write time and rejects the invalid order.
If queries often filter orders by customer_id, consider indexing that child column; PostgreSQL does not do so automatically.
blocks.outcome: The foreign key protects relationship integrity even when requests race. Indexing the referencing column is a separate performance decision.

blocks.text: A constraint puts a rule next to the data, where every writer must obey it.

Constraints are rules the database checks before accepting data. NOT NULL means a value is required; UNIQUE prevents duplicates; CHECK enforces a rule on one row; a foreign key checks a relationship. A default fills an omitted value, but does not stop an invalid value being supplied.

blocks.title: Encode rules close to the data
blocks.source:
CREATE TABLE payments (
  id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  order_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(id),
  amount NUMERIC(12,2) NOT NULL CHECK (amount > 0),
  currency CHAR(3) NOT NULL,
  status TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('pending', 'captured', 'failed'))
);

blocks.text: A CHECK constraint passes when its expression is TRUE or UNKNOWN; it rejects FALSE. Because comparisons with NULL commonly yield UNKNOWN, CHECK (amount > 0) does not itself prohibit NULL—use NOT NULL as well. A CHECK constraint is not a general cross-row or cross-table invariant. Use UNIQUE, FOREIGN KEY, exclusion constraints, or carefully designed transactional logic where appropriate.
Why application validation alone races

blocks.problem: Two requests try to create username 'sam' at almost the same time.
reasoning: Both requests can check first and see no matching username.
A UNIQUE constraint on username allows at most one conflicting insert to succeed.
Handle the uniqueness error as a normal conflict; do not rely on a prior SELECT as the guarantee.
blocks.outcome: Application validation improves the user message, while the database constraint provides the concurrency-safe guarantee.

concepts.title: Immediate and deferred constraints; safe concurrent writes

blocks.text: PostgreSQL usually checks a constraint as each SQL statement runs. A DEFERRABLE constraint can instead be checked later, typically when the transaction commits. This matters when a sequence of changes briefly breaks a rule even though the final result will be valid.

Immediate checking asks, “Is the data valid after this statement?” Deferred checking asks, “Is the data valid when this transaction is ready to commit?” Deferring does not remove the rule. It changes when PostgreSQL checks it.
### 1. Immediate checking: the default

Suppose Alice has seat 1 and Ben has seat 2. A UNIQUE constraint prevents two people from having the same seat. If you update Alice to seat 2 first, PostgreSQL sees a duplicate immediately and rejects the statement—even if you planned to move Ben to seat 1 next.

blocks.title: The first update fails with an ordinary UNIQUE constraint

blocks.text: The problem is the order of the updates, not the final arrangement. With immediate checking, PostgreSQL does not wait to see whether a later statement would repair the temporary duplicate.
### 2. Deferred checking: validate at commit

If swapping seat numbers is a legitimate operation, declare the UNIQUE constraint DEFERRABLE. Then defer it for this transaction. Both updates can temporarily create a duplicate, but the final values must be unique when you commit.

blocks.title: Swap two seat numbers with a deferred UNIQUE constraint

blocks.problem: After the first UPDATE, both people temporarily have seat 2. After the second UPDATE, Alice has seat 2 and Ben has seat 1.
reasoning: The constraint was declared DEFERRABLE, so PostgreSQL allows the transaction to continue after the temporary duplicate.
The second UPDATE restores uniqueness: each person has a different seat number.
At COMMIT, PostgreSQL checks the deferred constraint. If the duplicate remains, COMMIT fails.
blocks.outcome: Deferring changes the timing of the check, not the rule itself. The transaction must end with valid data.

blocks.text: ### 3. What must be true before you can defer a constraint?

The constraint must have been created as DEFERRABLE. SET CONSTRAINTS cannot make a NOT DEFERRABLE constraint deferrable. In PostgreSQL, PRIMARY KEY, UNIQUE, FOREIGN KEY, and EXCLUDE constraints can be declared DEFERRABLE; CHECK and NOT NULL cannot.

blocks.title: Change when a deferrable constraint is checked

blocks.text: INITIALLY IMMEDIATE means PostgreSQL checks after each statement unless you defer the constraint. INITIALLY DEFERRED means it starts deferred in each transaction. SET CONSTRAINTS ALL DEFERRED affects all eligible deferrable constraints; naming one constraint is often clearer.
### 4. When is deferring useful?

Use it when a valid operation needs a temporary invalid intermediate state—for example, swapping unique position numbers, renumbering rows, or inserting rows connected by circular foreign keys. It is not a way to ignore integrity rules, and it is unnecessary when every statement can keep the data valid on its own.

blocks.title: A deferred check can still fail
blocks.content: PostgreSQL can accept the statements and then reject COMMIT because the final data still violates the constraint. Application code must handle commit-time errors too. Inside an explicit transaction, a failed statement normally leaves the transaction in an error state until rollback or recovery to a savepoint.

blocks.text: ### 5. Concurrent requests are a different problem

Deferring a constraint is not the same as protecting a check-then-write race. Two registration requests can both SELECT a username, see no row, and then try to insert it. A transaction around each request does not by itself guarantee uniqueness.

blocks.title: Let a UNIQUE constraint arbitrate competing inserts

blocks.text: The UNIQUE rule is enforced by PostgreSQL even when requests arrive at the same time. One insert can claim the username; the conflicting insert cannot create a duplicate. ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING treats that conflict as an expected outcome; an API could instead return a clear “username already taken” response.

blocks.problem: A bank transfer subtracts $50 from account A and adds $50 to account B.
reasoning: Put both balance updates in one transaction so they commit together or roll back together.
A CHECK constraint can reject a negative balance, but it does not by itself prevent every lost update or concurrent-transfer problem.
Use safe update logic and appropriate row locking or transaction isolation when concurrent transfers can touch the same accounts.
blocks.outcome: Transactions keep related writes atomic. Constraints enforce specific data rules. Concurrency control protects operations whose correctness depends on other transactions.

columns: What it does not do by itself
rows: UNIQUE constraint
Prevents duplicate values or combinations, including under concurrent writes.
Does not explain the conflict to the user; the application still handles the result.
Transaction
Commits related changes together or rolls them back together.
Does not automatically prevent every race or define business rules.
DEFERRABLE constraint
Allows an eligible constraint check to be postponed.
Does not permit invalid data to be committed.
Locking / isolation
Coordinates concurrent operations according to the chosen strategy.
Does not replace durable constraints such as uniqueness.

blocks.text: ### Add a uniqueness rule safely on a busy table

Adding a unique constraint is not only a DDL operation; it is a data cleanup and deployment problem. First find existing duplicates, decide how to resolve them, and account for writes that can create new duplicates while the migration is running. For a large live PostgreSQL table, one common path is to build a unique index concurrently, verify that it is valid, then attach it as a constraint. The details depend on version, partitioning, and the exact constraint.

blocks.source:
-- Step 1: find duplicate business keys before the migration
SELECT email, count(*) AS row_count
FROM users
GROUP BY email
HAVING count(*) > 1
ORDER BY row_count DESC
LIMIT 100;

-- Step 2: after duplicates are resolved and new duplicates are prevented,
-- build a unique index while allowing ordinary writes to continue.
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY users_email_uq_idx
ON users (email);

-- Step 3: attach the existing index as a named constraint.
ALTER TABLE users
ADD CONSTRAINT users_email_key UNIQUE USING INDEX users_email_uq_idx;
blocks.title: Safe deployment pattern for a unique constraint

blocks.text: `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` cannot run inside an explicit transaction block. It performs more work and takes longer than a regular index build. If it fails, it can leave an INVALID index that is ignored by queries but still adds write overhead; inspect `pg_index.indisvalid`, drop the invalid index, resolve the cause, and retry. The precheck alone is not enough if writes can insert duplicates during the gap, so coordinate application validation or a staged write rule until uniqueness enforcement is active. Monitor lock waits, replication lag, and index-build progress.
1. Problem and motivation — Two requests try to register the same email at nearly the same time. A SELECT-before-INSERT check can let both through because neither request reserves the missing email.

2. Definition and design choice — Primary and foreign keys express identity and relationships; UNIQUE, NOT NULL, and CHECK constraints protect business rules at the database boundary. Application validation improves messages but cannot replace concurrency-safe constraints.

steps.title: Identify the fact
steps.description: Choose the entity and its stable identity, such as customer_id for a customer.

steps.title: Represent relationships
steps.description: Store a foreign key such as orders.customer_id that points to the owning customer.

steps.title: Declare invariants
steps.description: Use PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, UNIQUE, NOT NULL, and CHECK constraints for rules the database can enforce.

steps.title: Commit atomically
steps.description: A transaction groups related changes so observers do not see a half-finished business operation.

blocks.problem: Two requests both check for `sam@example.com`, see no row, and then attempt to insert it.
reasoning: Without a unique constraint, both inserts can succeed even though each request checked first; the checks raced.
A UNIQUE constraint makes the database arbitrate the conflict: one insert succeeds and the other gets a uniqueness violation.
Translate that error into a friendly response and decide whether retries are safe. Do not catch and ignore every constraint error.
blocks.outcome: Enforce durable invariants in the database, keep application validation for user experience, and test concurrent requests—not just sequential examples.

blocks.title: 5. Anti-pattern to avoid
blocks.content: Do not treat an application-side existence check as a substitute for UNIQUE, or use a foreign key only as documentation. Concurrent writers and alternate write paths can bypass those assumptions.

blocks.prompt: 6. Interview probe — How would you guarantee that every order belongs to a real customer and that two concurrent requests cannot create duplicate customer emails?
blocks.answer: Use a primary key for customer identity, a foreign key from orders to customers, and a UNIQUE constraint on the normalized email representation. Handle the expected uniqueness error in the application.
blocks.explanation: The database is the shared consistency boundary. Application checks improve user experience, but constraints enforce invariants under concurrency.

tradeoffsAndPitfalls.title: Surrogate key versus natural key
tradeoffsAndPitfalls.content:
Trade-off: Surrogate keys provide stable, compact references; natural keys can express real business uniqueness directly.

Failure mode: A surrogate ID is mistaken for sufficient integrity, allowing duplicate business entities.

Decision rule: Use a stable primary key for row identity and separately constrain genuine business keys. Prefer natural keys as primary keys only when their uniqueness, stability, and scope are well understood.

tradeoffsAndPitfalls.title: Foreign keys versus application-managed references
tradeoffsAndPitfalls.content:
Trade-off: Foreign keys provide strong integrity but can constrain deletion order, migrations, and cross-database boundaries.

Failure mode: Application-only checks permit orphaned rows during concurrent writes or from a background job.

Decision rule: Use database foreign keys for relationships within the same database unless a deliberate architectural constraint justifies otherwise; then document and monitor the compensating integrity mechanism.

tradeoffsAndPitfalls.title: CASCADE versus RESTRICT
tradeoffsAndPitfalls.content:
Trade-off: CASCADE simplifies dependent cleanup; RESTRICT makes destructive consequences explicit.

Failure mode: A cascade deletes historical or independently meaningful data.

Decision rule: Choose based on lifecycle and retention rules, not convenience. Test deletion behavior on representative relationship graphs.

tradeoffsAndPitfalls.title: Validation in application versus database
tradeoffsAndPitfalls.content:
Trade-off: Application validation yields friendly errors; database constraints protect all writers and close race conditions.

Failure mode: A check-then-insert flow creates duplicates because two requests pass validation simultaneously.

Decision rule: Use both: validate early for UX, enforce durable invariants in the database, and handle constraint violations as expected outcomes.

tradeoffsAndPitfalls.title: CHECK versus cross-row logic
tradeoffsAndPitfalls.content:
Trade-off: CHECK is simple and efficient for row-local predicates but cannot safely enforce arbitrary aggregates across rows.

Failure mode: A CHECK function or application query attempts to enforce a total limit across concurrent rows without concurrency control.

Decision rule: Use UNIQUE/FK/exclusion constraints where possible; for aggregate invariants, design explicit locking, serializable transactions, or a normalized representation that makes the invariant enforceable.

revisionSheet.text:
What does a primary key guarantee?

Answer: Uniqueness and non-NULL identity for each row. It does not automatically enforce every business uniqueness rule.

What is a candidate key?

Answer: A minimal attribute set that uniquely identifies a row. The chosen candidate key is the primary key; other candidate keys can be UNIQUE constraints.

Does PostgreSQL automatically index a foreign-key column?

Answer: No. The referenced key is indexed through its PRIMARY KEY or UNIQUE constraint, but the referencing columns are not automatically indexed.

CHECK (amount > 0) rejects NULL—is that true?

Answer: No. A CHECK passes for TRUE or UNKNOWN. Pair it with NOT NULL when NULL is invalid.

When should ON DELETE CASCADE be used?

Answer: When child rows have no independent lifecycle and parent deletion should intentionally delete them too.

Why isn't checking uniqueness in application code enough?

Answer: Concurrent requests can both observe that a value is absent. A database UNIQUE constraint serializes the invariant at the write boundary.

Can every constraint be deferred?

Answer: No. In PostgreSQL, CHECK and NOT NULL are not deferrable; selected key, foreign-key, and exclusion constraints can be.

What should application code do after a constraint violation inside a transaction?

Answer: Treat the transaction as failed, roll it back or recover to a savepoint, and translate known violations into a safe domain-level response.

questions.prompt: Which design best prevents duplicate accounts when two requests register the same email concurrently?

options.text: Check for the email in the API before inserting.
Use a UNIQUE constraint for the product's email identity rule and handle conflicts.
Wrap each API request in a transaction without any constraint.
Use a UUID primary key and no email constraint.

questions.explanation: A database uniqueness constraint enforces the invariant across concurrent writers. An application pre-check can improve the message but cannot close the race by itself.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, what happens when a CHECK expression evaluates to UNKNOWN because a referenced value is NULL?

options.text: The row is rejected.
The row passes that CHECK constraint.
PostgreSQL silently converts NULL to zero.
The constraint is ignored for every future update.

questions.explanation: CHECK rejects FALSE; TRUE and UNKNOWN satisfy it. Add NOT NULL when nullability is forbidden.

questions.prompt: Which statements about PostgreSQL foreign keys are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: They can prevent orphaned references.
The referenced key must be backed by a suitable unique key.
PostgreSQL automatically indexes every referencing column.
ON DELETE CASCADE should reflect an intentional lifecycle rule.

questions.explanation: Foreign keys protect referential integrity; the referenced columns need an eligible unique key. PostgreSQL does not automatically index the referencing columns.

questions.prompt: A transaction around a check-then-insert sequence guarantees that two concurrent requests cannot create the same business key.
questions.explanation: A transaction alone does not necessarily serialize that invariant. Enforce uniqueness in the database and handle a conflict.

questions.prompt: A service checks whether username 'aman' exists, then inserts it if absent. Two requests can run concurrently. What is the correct diagnosis?

options.text: The existence check makes the operation atomic.
Both requests can observe no row; enforce uniqueness with a UNIQUE constraint/index and handle conflicts.
A foreign key on username prevents duplicates.
A sleep between SELECT and INSERT guarantees correctness.

questions.explanation: The check and insert are separate operations. A database-enforced unique constraint/index is authoritative; handle conflicts or use an atomic upsert.

questions.prompt: A table must enforce that each active subscription has at most one row per (account_id, plan_id). Which constraint best expresses this invariant?

options.text: A CHECK constraint that compares account_id and plan_id
A UNIQUE constraint on (account_id, plan_id)
A foreign key from account_id to plan_id
A default value for subscription_id

questions.explanation: Uniqueness across a combination of columns is the job of a composite UNIQUE constraint. A CHECK constraint is row-local and does not safely compare other rows.
questions.hint: Ask whether the rule concerns one row or a set of rows.

questions.prompt: Which statements about keys and constraints are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: A candidate key is a minimal set of attributes that uniquely identifies a row.
A surrogate primary key removes the need to enforce business-key uniqueness.
A foreign key can enforce that a child references an eligible parent key.
A primary key permits multiple NULL values if the database supports NULLs.

questions.explanation: Candidate keys are minimal unique identifiers, and foreign keys protect references. A primary key is unique and NOT NULL; surrogate identity does not replace business uniqueness.

questions.prompt: A PostgreSQL CHECK (quantity > 0) constraint alone guarantees that quantity cannot be NULL.
questions.explanation: A CHECK passes when its expression is TRUE or UNKNOWN. Pair CHECK with NOT NULL when NULL is forbidden.

questions.prompt: You need to delete a customer only if no orders reference them. Which referential action best matches that rule?

options.text: ON DELETE CASCADE
ON DELETE SET NULL
ON DELETE RESTRICT or an equivalent NO ACTION rule
ON UPDATE CASCADE

questions.explanation: RESTRICT/NO ACTION prevents deleting a referenced parent while dependent rows remain. CASCADE would delete the orders, which is a different lifecycle decision.

questions.prompt: A migration adds a UNIQUE constraint to a large production table. Which steps are sensible? Select all that apply.

options.text: Find and resolve existing duplicate values before enforcement.
Check database-specific locking and index-build behavior.
Assume the application pre-check guarantees no duplicates during rollout.
Plan how concurrent writes and constraint failures will be handled.

questions.explanation: Existing duplicates can prevent the constraint from being created. Production rollout also needs an operational plan for locks, concurrent writes, and conflict handling.

questions.prompt: Two concurrent transactions reserve the same seat. Each checks availability before inserting a reservation. What is the strongest general protection against duplicate active reservations?

options.text: A longer transaction timeout
A database uniqueness rule that encodes the seat's reservation scope, with conflict handling
A second availability SELECT after the first SELECT
A random delay before insert

questions.explanation: A database constraint is the authoritative concurrency boundary. The exact key may include event_id, seat_id, and reservation state depending on the lifecycle model.

questions.prompt: Wrapping a read-check-write sequence in a transaction automatically prevents every race between concurrent transactions.
questions.explanation: Transactions provide atomicity for each transaction, but they do not automatically enforce all cross-transaction invariants. Constraints, locking, or suitable isolation may still be required.

interviewScenarios.prompt: Two API instances can create users concurrently. The product requires each normalized email to identify at most one account. Design the schema and describe the write path.
strongAnswerPoints: Choose a stable user primary key separate from the mutable email value.
Define the product's email normalization and case-sensitivity policy explicitly.
Enforce the resulting uniqueness rule with an appropriate database constraint or unique index.
Do not rely on a pre-insert SELECT as the correctness mechanism.
Handle uniqueness violations as a domain conflict and avoid exposing raw SQL errors.
Consider how existing duplicates are detected and resolved before adding the constraint.
pitfalls: Claiming a transaction automatically prevents duplicates.
Ignoring case normalization and existing data cleanup.
Treating every database exception as the same error.
interviewScenarios.referenceAnswer: I would use a stable user ID as the primary key and enforce the email identity rule in the database. First I would define normalization and case-sensitivity semantics, then clean existing conflicting data and add the corresponding uniqueness constraint or unique index. The API may pre-check to give a friendly message, but the insert is authoritative: concurrent requests can race. I would catch the specific uniqueness conflict and return a safe domain-level response. I would also plan deployment carefully if the table is large, because building the constraint/index and resolving legacy duplicates need an operational migration plan.

interviewScenarios.prompt: Model a ticket-booking system where one seat can be reserved once per show, users can cancel reservations, and reservation attempts may arrive concurrently. Explain the schema invariants and write-path behavior.
strongAnswerPoints: Define the reservation row grain and stable primary key.
Use foreign keys to reference a show, seat, and user where those entities live in the same database.
Enforce one active reservation per show and seat using a suitable database uniqueness strategy, accounting for cancelled rows if needed.
Treat availability checks as user experience, not the concurrency guarantee.
Handle unique conflicts or serialization failures as expected domain outcomes.
Explain how cancellation and re-reservation affect the invariant and any partial unique index.
pitfalls: Relying only on a SELECT availability check.
Using a global UNIQUE(seat_id) when seats can be booked for different shows.
Ignoring cancellation semantics or retry behavior.
interviewScenarios.referenceAnswer: I would define one reservation row per booking attempt or current reservation, then enforce the business rule at the database boundary. If cancelled reservations remain for history, a partial unique index on (show_id, seat_id) for active reservations may express the invariant in PostgreSQL; alternatively, model current occupancy separately. The API can check availability for a friendly response, but concurrent requests still race, so the insert/update must handle a uniqueness conflict. Foreign keys protect references, and cancellation must release the active uniqueness slot without erasing audit history.

description: Relational Databases, Primary Keys, Foreign Keys, and Constraints. Interview-focused explanations, worked examples, trade-offs, and practice.
